title: Parliament unprorogued for 102 days with no Winter Session dates; Congress alleges 'something sinister'
dek: The Monsoon Session, adjourned on 13 August, has still not been formally closed. The Opposition links the delay to the failed delimitation bill; the government says it has broken no rule.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Congress on Monday accused the Union government of planning "something truly sinister" by keeping Parliament's Monsoon Session open for more than three months without announcing a Winter Session, as the gap since both Houses last sat reached 102 days with no word from the government on when they will meet again.

The Monsoon Session ran from 20 July to 13 August, when both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha were adjourned sine die. The session has not been prorogued, the formal step that ends it, and the government has not announced dates for the Winter Session, which in most years begins in late November or early December.

## What the Opposition says

Jairam Ramesh, the Congress general secretary in charge of communications, wrote in a post on X on Monday morning that "by now, the nation should have known when the Winter Session of Parliament will take place", or when the unprorogued Monsoon Session would be reconvened. He said "the nation is entitled to know" the government's formula for delimitation, and asked "what games are being played" by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah. He also renewed his party's attack on the Chief Election Commissioner over the revision of electoral rolls.

The Congress alleges that the government is keeping the session open so that it can recall Parliament at short notice once it is sure of a two-thirds majority for a fresh delimitation bill, and that it may skip a Winter Session altogether to avoid questions on the electoral-roll revision, according to reports. These are the party's claims; the government has not said what it plans.

Other Opposition parties have made similar complaints. Derek O'Brien, the Trinamool Congress leader in the Rajya Sabha, wrote on 20 November that the government "will not have even a single day of Parliament in November". CPI(M) MP John Brittas said the same day that there were "no dates" and "no consultation", according to reports.

## What the government says

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju has said that leaving a session open breaks no rule. In an interview in August he said summoning Parliament was "entirely up to the government", that "as long as the session has not been officially ended, it can be reconvened", and that the government was "not doing anything new", citing earlier cases since 1952, according to reports. In an October letter to the Congress leader Mallikarjun Kharge, he wrote that not proroguing did not give rise to "any constitutional or procedural impropriety or irregularity", and that the government had already discussed the delimitation bill with the Opposition, according to reports. The government had not responded to Monday's post by the time of publication.

## Background

The Constitution sets no deadline for prorogation, but Article 85 requires that no more than six months pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next, which puts the outer limit for the next sitting in mid-February. The longest earlier gap before prorogation was 87 days, in 2008, according to reports.

Last year the government announced on 8 November that the Winter Session would run from 1 to 19 December. Reports this month, citing unnamed officials, said a session was likely to begin in the first week of December; nothing has been confirmed.

The dispute is tied to the delimitation package. On 17 April the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which would have raised the Lok Sabha's size to as many as 850 seats and linked it to one-third reservation for women before the 2029 election, won 298 votes to 230 but fell short of the two-thirds majority of members present and voting that it needed. Reports since then say the government is considering a revised formula that would raise every state's seats by 50% while keeping their shares unchanged. The Congress says it is not against delimitation but wants an all-party meeting first.

## What happens next

The government can either reconvene the Monsoon Session at short notice or prorogue it and summon a new session, which normally means about two weeks' notice to members. If the Winter Session is to start in early December, an announcement would have to come within days.
